components.text: The demand that supernatural reality must enter as a gap in natural mechanisms is rejected as a mistaken model of divine activity.
Whether natural mechanisms are compatible with an omnipresent divine cause is directly addressed.
Whether empirical natural mechanisms make divine activity explanatorily unnecessary.
The claimed continuing role for something outside nature is answered by presenting plausible cosmological models that are physically self-contained.
The distinction between physical models and metaphysical interpretation is indirectly engaged, but no direct criterion for excluding divine compatibility is supplied.
Whether cosmology requires an origin mechanism outside the natural system.
Whether physical self-containment is incompatible with concurrent divine activity.
The expectation that revelation should disclose scientific structure is replaced with an empiricist demand appropriate to a freely created contingent world.
The existence of lawful self-contained mechanisms is treated as discoverable through observation rather than deducible from divine nature.
Why a theistic worldview should rely on empirical inquiry rather than revealed scientific detail.
Whether divine freedom remains compatible with self-contained cosmological laws.
The explanatory demand concerning life-permitting conditions is met with environmental selection across varied domains.
The move offers a physical explanatory proposal rather than relying on a metaphysical design gloss.
The contingency of natural laws is relevant, but the revelation and divine-freedom argument is not directly answered.
Whether complete natural mechanisms exclude or merely coexist with divine activity.
Whether a compact physical account can explain apparently special cosmic conditions.
The probabilistic inference is challenged because its possibility space and probability measure are not adequately established.
Self-contained cosmological possibility is not denied, but its bearing on comparative metaphysical probability is questioned.
The move models revisability by lowering confidence when a supporting argument fails.
Whether fine-tuning probabilities support a well-founded metaphysical conclusion.
Whether physical explanation by itself determines the appropriate prior credence in divine purpose.
The broader naturalist appeal to self-contained physical explanation is contacted through self-contained quantum models requiring no nonphysical minds.
The analogy to self-contained cosmology is explicit and supports compatibility with materialism.
The move supports restraint in drawing metaphysical conclusions from scientific theory.
Whether naturalistic selection supplies an adequate explanation of fine-tuning.
Whether quantum mechanics requires departure from a natural or material ontology.
The claim that quantum mechanics is compatible with materialism is expressly accepted and restated.
General caution about drawing metaphysical conclusions from physics is mirrored, though fine-tuning probabilities are not addressed.
Compatibility rather than exclusion is the operative inference, so divine compatibility is not defeated.
Whether quantum mechanics has foundational implications that rule out materialism.
Whether interpretive choices should be distinguished from the empirical content of quantum theory.
The inference from successful physical explanation to exhaustive reduction of persons is resisted by distinguishing evidence for physical explanation from metaphysical necessity.
Compatibility of physics with materialism is granted, while the stronger claim that materialism is required is denied.
The naturalist claim that the rule-governed natural world exhausts reality is challenged as underdetermined by current evidence.
Whether a successful physical or emergent account settles the metaphysical status of persons.
Whether compatibility with materialism establishes that persons are only material.
The inference from a favored deterministic physical interpretation to a settled conclusion about agency is defeated by interpretive underdetermination.
The absence of a unique metaphysical implication from quantum mechanics is directly reinforced.
The broader move from scientific data to an exclusive worldview is challenged as underdetermined.
Whether fundamental physics determines the truth or falsity of free will.
Whether competing quantum interpretations support a unique metaphysical conclusion.
The epistemic demand for model-based inquiry is accepted while its metaphysical consequence is questioned.
Quantum modeling is treated as compatible with multiple metaphysical descriptions, directly supporting restraint.
The possibility of a mathematically modeled higher-level phenomenon is acknowledged, though agency itself is not addressed.
Whether successful mathematical and empirical modeling uniquely supports a naturalist metaphysics.
Whether a consciousness variable in a quantum model would necessarily be non-natural.
The demand for an account of consciousness is answered by locating it within an unfinished neuroscience and prospective mapping program.
The claim that current science does not settle personhood is partly conceded through acknowledgment that consciousness remains difficult.
The move concerns consciousness rather than the neutrality of physics on agency.
Whether consciousness presently supplies a reason to posit something beyond physicalism.
Whether successful brain-state mapping would support a physical account despite present incompleteness.
The denial of a real external standard is answered by affirming a standard disclosed through recognition of personal moral failure.
The introspective focus is adjacent to consciousness but does not answer the neuroscience claim.
Self-examination supplies a form of correction, though it is not tied to empirical equilibrium.
Whether morality is merely constructed or answers to a real standard beyond individual preference.
Whether a real moral order requires a culturally invariant detailed rulebook.
The demand for a source of value and moral seriousness is answered through finite relationships and shared present experience.
The status of persons beyond physical life is denied rather than independently argued in this span.
The move presents a naturalist interpretation of meaning but does not revisit the fact-versus-gloss distinction.
Whether human moral failure points to a real standard and a need for transcendent help.
Whether value and meaning require an afterlife or transcendent completion.
The demand that present life matter only if there is no afterlife is replaced by a demand that mature theism value present life while retaining hope beyond it.
Plural worthwhile callings contact humanly grounded value, though the metaethical construction claim is not directly answered.
The critique of immature life-devaluing theism is accepted as a correction within a revisable worldview.
The willingness to correct a mistaken conception parallels revisability but does not supply empirical verification of afterlife hope.
Whether belief in an afterlife intrinsically devalues present life.
Whether scientific work is the exclusive paradigm of meaningful vocation.
Whether plural worthwhile callings can be recognized within a theistic normative order.
